title: Cover
lines: A guided workbook for understanding your style, your clothes, and the way you want to get dressed.

title: Opening Note
lines: Getting dressed is something we do almost every day, yet many women reach adulthood without ever being taught how to understand their own preferences.
They know what looks good on someone else.
They know what they are “supposed” to own.
why certain outfits feel like them;
what their life actually requires from their clothes.
You are not here to find the “right” style.
You are here to understand your own.
Personal style grows through repeated observation, preference, experience, and real life. This workbook gives you a way to look at those things more deliberately.

title: What This Blueprint Is
lines: THIS IS NOT A STYLE QUIZ.
The Blueprint does not assign you a body type, an aesthetic, a fashion personality, a fixed colour season, or a list of clothes you “should” wear.
Instead, it helps you examine evidence from your own life.
What do I naturally respond to visually?
What does my actual life require?
There are no perfect answers here. There are only patterns worth noticing.

title: How to Use It
lines: Pay attention to what you already wear, save, notice, avoid, and enjoy.
Make specific selections instead of answering vaguely.
Look for what your choices might be telling you.
Turn those observations into something you can actually use.
Don't answer according to what you think you should like.

Move through the workbook in order. Each part builds on the discoveries you made in the part before it. When a page asks you to interpret your answers, use the prompts as guidance—not as a verdict. Your answers may point to a clear preference, a combination of preferences, or something you are still figuring out.
The goal is not to force yourself into one category. It is to build a clearer understanding of your personal style.

title: Your Evidence Sets
lines: Collect 8–12 outfits you have actually worn.
They can include photos of yourself, mirror selfies, screenshots, or outfits you remember clearly.
Include a mixture if possible: outfits you loved, outfits you liked, ordinary outfits, outfits you felt uncomfortable in, and outfits you would not repeat.
Don't choose only outfits you think look good. We're not building a highlight reel. We're trying to discover your patterns.
Collect 10–15 outfits or images that genuinely made you stop and look.
They do not need to be outfits you would wear. You will interpret what caught your attention later.
Think about where you actually go, what you do, what your days look like, and what your clothing needs to help you accomplish.
Do not create a new evidence set every time a page asks you to reflect. Reuse these same sets throughout the workbook.

title: Before You Begin
lines: Your body is not a rulebook.
Your inspiration is not automatically your style.
Your lifestyle is not the life you think you should have.
Your answers do not need to fit neatly into one category.
☐ Enough time to think without rushing
☐ No need to get every answer “right”
The goal is not to create a perfect description of yourself. The goal is to become better at seeing yourself.

title: Your Body
lines: This section isn't about finding your “body type” or learning which clothes you're supposed to wear.
It's about noticing what actually works for you.
Your body affects how clothes fit, sit, move, and create shape. But there isn't one correct way for clothes to look on your body.
The goal is to understand your own patterns:
By the end of this section, you'll have a clearer understanding of your preferred fit, silhouettes, proportions, lengths, necklines, skin exposure, and physical comfort.

title: Fit
lines: What Does “Good Fit” Actually Mean to You?
Fit isn't simply about whether something technically fits your measurements.
It's also about how close you enjoy clothing sitting against your body.
Two people can wear the same size and prefer completely different levels of closeness.
For each outfit, identify the dominant fit.
Follows the body without feeling tight.
Has noticeable room without looking oversized.
Falls away from the body with plenty of room.
Intentionally large and generous in proportion.
Now mark how you feel about each fit:
Which fits appear most often in outfits you enjoy wearing?
Which ones do you repeatedly avoid?
And is there a difference between:
The fits I naturally gravitate towards:
The fits I tend to avoid:

title: Fit Observation
lines: Now step back from individual outfits.
Complete these statements based on what you just observed.
I feel most comfortable when my clothes are:
I tend to dislike clothes that:
☐ Emphasise my body more than I want
☐ Hide too much of my shape
☐ Make me feel swallowed by the fabric
I feel most like myself when my clothes ________.
Your goal isn't to choose one correct fit.
Your goal is to understand the range of fit that feels natural to you.

title: Fit Interpretation
lines: WHAT YOUR FIT PATTERN MAY TELL YOU
Which fit appeared most often among the outfits you loved?
Which fit did you repeatedly avoid?
Did you prefer one fit everywhere, or did you prefer different fits for different garments?
Did a particular combination keep appearing?
You don't need to choose one “correct” fit. You're looking for the fit patterns that repeatedly make you feel comfortable and like yourself.

title: Silhouette
lines: What Shape Do Your Clothes Create?
Fit tells us how closely clothes sit on your body.
Silhouette looks at the bigger picture.
It's the overall shape created by your clothes when you look at the outfit as a whole.
You might love a relaxed top with a defined bottom.
You might prefer a streamlined outfit from head to toe.
You might enjoy oversized pieces — but only when something else creates balance.
We're looking for your repeated preferences.
A relatively consistent width through the outfit.
The shape of the body is intentionally visible.
Soft, easy shapes with room to move.
Generous volume creates the dominant shape.
One part follows the body while another is more relaxed.
A shorter piece is paired with a longer piece to create contrast.
Longer pieces create an elongated, relatively clean shape.
~ MAYBE — I like something about it
“Would I actually want to wear this?”

title: Silhouette Comparison
lines: Look at the silhouettes you marked YES.
What do they have in common?
☐ A combination of fitted and relaxed
The silhouette direction I naturally gravitate towards:
A silhouette combination I repeatedly enjoy:
A silhouette direction I tend to avoid:

title: Lengths and Proportions
lines: It's Not Just the Pieces. It's the Relationship Between Them.
An outfit can contain pieces you individually love and still feel wrong when they're combined.
Proportion is about how the lengths and volumes of different pieces relate to one another.
None of these combinations is automatically better.
We're simply going to see which relationships you repeatedly enjoy.
Which combinations make your outfits feel most natural?
Which combinations consistently feel “off” to you?

title: Lengths and Proportions: Choose
lines: Where Do You Naturally Like Your Clothes to End?
Look through your recent outfits and identify the lengths you repeatedly choose.
You may notice that your preferences aren't consistent across every garment.
“Where do I repeatedly feel most like myself?”
A length I thought I liked but rarely actually wear:

title: Necklines and Openings
lines: How Do You Like Your Upper Body Framed?
Necklines can change the entire feeling of an outfit.
But again, there isn't a universally “best” neckline.
We're interested in what you actually enjoy seeing and wearing.
Put each into one of four groups:
I admire this on other people

title: Neckline Preferences
lines: Something I noticed about how I like my upper body framed:

title: Skin Exposure
lines: How Much Do You Actually Like to Show?
Some people feel best when they're mostly covered.
Some enjoy showing their legs but not their chest.
Someone else might be comfortable showing shoulders but not their stomach.
The goal is to identify your own boundary.

title: Skin Exposure: Choose
lines: What kind of exposure feels most natural to you?
I feel most comfortable with clothing that shows ______ while keeping ______ relatively covered.

title: Comfort and Movement
lines: What Does Your Body Need From Your Clothes?
Style isn't useful if you're uncomfortable all day.
Think about what makes you physically aware of your clothes in a negative way.
☐ Make me worry about wardrobe malfunctions
☐ Comfortable enough for a few hours
☐ Worth some discomfort for the right outfit
Which discomforts are automatic no's for you?
Something I'm willing to compromise on occasionally:

You are not leaving this section with a list of rules telling you what your body should wear. You're leaving with evidence about the physical qualities that make clothing feel natural, comfortable, and right to you.
Next, we'll look beyond how clothes work on your body and explore what you want your clothes to look and feel like.

title: Your Personality
lines: For this section, we're going to use visual evidence.
You don't need to know the name of your style.
You don't need to decide whether you're “classic,” “romantic,” “minimalist,” “edgy,” or any other style category.
Instead, we're going to look at what repeatedly catches your attention.
Because sometimes your style is easier to discover by noticing:
«“Why did I stop scrolling when I saw this?”»
Create a collection of 10–15 outfits that caught your attention.
- people you see in real life
- anywhere else you naturally find style inspiration
They don't all need to look alike.
Choose them because something about them made you stop and look.

title: Inspiration Set
lines: Collect 10–15 outfits that made you stop and look.
They can come from: Pinterest; Instagram; people you know; celebrities; old photos of yourself; outfits you've worn; outfits you've saved; real life.
Don't choose outfits because you think they are “your style.” Choose them because something about them caught your attention.
Maybe it was the silhouette, the proportions, the colour, the neckline, the texture, the styling, the shoes, the accessories, the level of detail, or the overall feeling.
You don't need to know why yet. That's what we're going to discover.
Your job: Collect first. Interpret later.

title: What Caught Your Eye?
lines: Now go through your 10–15 outfits again.
It might be the overall outfit.
Or it might be one tiny detail.
Which five visual qualities appear repeatedly across your inspiration?
Look at the five qualities you identified.
Which of these do I actually want in my own wardrobe?
Visual quality| I want this often| I want this sometimes| I like seeing it, but not wearing it
Are there any qualities that appear frequently in your inspiration but rarely appear in your actual clothes?
Why do you think that might be?
Are there qualities you already wear without consciously realizing they're part of your style?
«The visual qualities I naturally want more of are:»
«The visual qualities I enjoy admiring but don't necessarily need to wear are:»

title: Admiration Is Not Personal Style
lines: Something Can Be Beautiful Without Being You
This is one of the most important exercises in the Blueprint.
You can look at someone else's outfit and think:
And still never want to wear it.
You can admire a dramatic outfit without wanting a dramatic wardrobe.
You can love a minimalist outfit without wanting to dress minimally every day.
You can appreciate a style that looks incredible on someone else and still know:
Go through your 10–15 saved outfits and place each one into one of these categories:
I love it, and I can genuinely imagine myself wearing it.
I think it's beautiful, but I don't actually want to dress this way.
Something about it appeals to me, but I'm not sure yet.
I don't particularly want this direction.
Look at your BEAUTIFUL + NOT ME group.
What makes these outfits appealing even though you don't want to wear them?
Now look at your BEAUTIFUL + ME group.
What do you want to take from them?
«Something I admire but don't actually want for myself is:»
«Something I repeatedly see and think “that's me” is:»
«A style direction I might have confused with my personal style is:»

title: Visual Dials
lines: Style isn't always one thing or the other.
You might be minimalist but still want visual interest.
You might like feminine clothes without wanting to look overly romantic.
You might like polished outfits but still want them to feel relaxed.
Instead of forcing yourself into a label, use these visual dials to describe your preferences.
Where do you naturally prefer to be?
You don't have to choose an extreme.
relaxed in everyday life + polished when you want to dress up.
Your answers are describing a range, not assigning you a type.

title: Visual Intensity
lines: Some outfits need very little to feel complete.
Others need colour, texture, jewellery, layering, contrast, or another point of interest.
Think about your ideal everyday outfit.
Few elements. Very little visual information.
Mostly simple, with one noticeable element.
Several things create visual interest, but the outfit still feels controlled.
Colour, texture, contrast, accessories, layering, or statement pieces are all welcome.
☐ It changes depending on the occasion
How much visual interest feels like enough?
When does an outfit start feeling too plain?
When does an outfit start feeling like too much?
What is usually the easiest way for you to add interest?
«My ideal amount of visual interest is:»

title: Femininity, Polish, and Edge
lines: Three Qualities That Can Change the Feeling of an Outfit
You don't have to choose whether your style is “feminine” or “edgy.”
Your style can hold combinations that seem contradictory.
Let's see where you naturally sit.
Where do you naturally prefer to be?
Classic / Subtle ───── Slightly Unexpected ───── Strongly Edgy
«I like femininity when it feels ______ rather than ______.»
«I like looking polished, but I don't want my style to feel ______.»
My balance of femininity, polish and edge:

title: Colour: Natural Direction
lines: What Colours Do You Actually Want to Wear?
Liking a colour doesn't automatically mean you need it in your wardrobe.
You might love bright pink but rarely reach for it.
You might admire orange but discover that it works best as a small accent.
You might own lots of black because it's easy, even though you actually want more colour.
So we're going to look at your relationship with colour, not simply your favourite colours.
What colours do you naturally repeat?
Are there colours you love in theory but don't enjoy wearing?
Are there colours you wear because they're easy rather than because they feel like you?

title: Six-Colour Formula
lines: You don't need a wardrobe full of every colour you like.
You need a colour system that helps your wardrobe feel cohesive while still allowing personality.
Your Six-Colour Formula gives each colour a role.
Black, navy, cream, brown, charcoal, denim, or another colour that naturally anchors your wardrobe.
A second colour that works easily with your anchor.
A lighter or softer neutral that gives your wardrobe another easy option.
A deeper or stronger neutral that adds contrast.
A less predictable colour that adds personality.
A colour that can become recognisably yours through smaller details, accessories, shoes, beauty, or occasional clothing.
Your Six-Colour Formula is not a six-colour wardrobe restriction.
These six roles simply help you understand which colours feel foundational, supportive, flexible or distinctive in your personal style.
You can wear colours outside your formula. The point is to understand your colour direction—not to create a rule you are afraid to break.

title: Build Your Six-Colour Formula
lines: Will This Colour Actually Work in Your Wardrobe?
A colour can be beautiful and still be difficult to use.
Before making it part of your wardrobe, apply the Rule of Three.
«Can this colour work with at least three things I already own?»
If yes, it has real wardrobe potential.
If no, it doesn't automatically mean you can't buy it.
It simply means you should understand that it may function as a special piece rather than an easy wardrobe colour.
☐ Beautiful but unnecessary for my wardrobe
«The overall colour direction I want my wardrobe to have is:»
«A colour I love but don't necessarily need is:»
The Rule of Three is a practicality check, not a permission slip.

title: Style Signatures
lines: What Do You Keep Doing Without Thinking?
Style signatures are the small things that repeatedly appear in your outfits.
Which things appear again and again?
Which are so automatic that you barely think about them?
Which ones make an outfit feel more like you?

title: Automatic and Deliberate Signatures
lines: Separate your signatures into two groups.
Things you repeatedly choose without consciously planning them.
Things you consciously add when you want the outfit to feel a certain way.
If you could keep only three recurring style signatures, which would you choose?
«My outfits often feel more like me when I add ______.»

title: Personality Style Profile
lines: You've explored what catches your eye, what you admire, what you actually want to wear, your visual preferences, visual intensity, colour direction, and style signatures. Use this page to collect the discoveries—not to decide on a permanent aesthetic label.
WHAT I ACTUALLY WANT TO WEAR:
I want my clothes to feel __________________ while looking __________________.

Part 1 showed you how clothes work on your body. Part 2 showed you what you want your style to look and feel like. The next part brings in another essential piece: the life your clothes need to support.

title: What Keeps Showing Up?
lines: Look back at your Inspiration Set, your visual-dial choices, your colour notes, and your style-signature observations. You do not need to find identical words. Look for details or ideas that seem related.
I feel most visually satisfied when an outfit has __________________.
My style becomes more recognisably mine when I add __________________.
I admire __________________, but I do not necessarily want to wear it.
Related preferences that may be pointing to the same thing:
Choose 3–5 qualities you genuinely want your clothes to express—not simply words that sound stylish.
Now combine the qualities in your own words.
The combination of qualities that feels most like me is __________________.
For example: feminine + relaxed + slightly edgy; or polished + simple + expressive. Your combination does not need to fit an existing style category. It only needs to make sense to you.
The visual direction I seem to be building is __________________.
A repeated detail or idea I want to remember is __________________.
These are working observations, not a final verdict. You will test them against your real life in the next part.

title: Your Lifestyle
lines: For this section, think about your real life, not your ideal life.
Think about the last few weeks or months.
What did you repeatedly need to wear?
You don't need to judge your lifestyle.
If you spend most of your time at home, that's useful information.
If your life is mostly casual, that's useful information.
If you regularly move between work, church, errands and social events, that's useful information too.
«“What kind of life would I like my wardrobe to represent?”»
«“What kind of life does my wardrobe actually need to support?”»

title: Where Do You Actually Go?
lines: Which of these situations do you actually dress for?
Now mark how often each one actually occurs.
Very frequent — part of normal life
Look at the categories you marked Very frequent and Frequent.
These are some of the most important contexts your wardrobe needs to serve.
My three most common dressing situations are:

title: Real-Life Time Map
lines: Where Does Your Time Actually Go?
Sometimes our wardrobes reflect the life we imagine rather than the life we spend most of our time living.
Imagine you have 100 points representing your typical week or month.
Divide the 100 points across the activities that actually make up your life.

title: Read Your Time Map
lines: Which categories take up the largest share of your life?
Which categories take up very little of your life?
If you looked at your wardrobe without knowing anything about you, would it reflect this time map?
Look at your three largest categories.
Ask: Are these also the areas my wardrobe needs to support most?
Then look at your smallest categories.
Am I giving a lot of wardrobe attention to situations that barely happen in my real life?
You are not being asked to change your wardrobe yet. You're simply noticing the relationship between how you actually spend your time and what your clothes need to support.
My three biggest real-life dressing contexts are:
The biggest mismatch I noticed is:

title: What Do You Actually Need to Get Dressed For?
lines: Knowing that you go to “work” or “errands” doesn't tell us everything your clothes need to do.
Think about the actual tasks and transitions involved.
- leaving home and returning several hours later
- moving between indoor and outdoor spaces
- going somewhere casual that could become social
- moving from work into an evening activity
- dressing appropriately without wanting to feel overdressed
LOOK AT YOUR THREE MOST COMMON SITUATIONS
What do your clothes need to help you do?
For each quality, decide whether it is:
The three things my clothes most need to help me do are:

title: Environment
lines: What Does Your Environment Actually Demand?
Your environment affects what makes clothing practical.
But not every environmental factor deserves equal weight.
Think about what genuinely affects your daily dressing.
Which environmental factors strongly affect what you can realistically wear?
You don't need to design your entire wardrobe around every possible condition.
Focus on the things that actually affect your everyday life.

title: What Does Practical Mean to You?
lines: Practical Doesn't Mean the Same Thing to Everyone

One person considers a garment practical because it's comfortable. Another cares about whether it survives frequent washing. Someone else values pieces that work with many outfits or are easy to put on and style.
Don't assume you need someone else's definition of practicality. Build your own.
Place each quality into one of four groups: NON-NEGOTIABLE / IMPORTANT / NICE TO HAVE / I DON'T REALLY CARE.
☐ Easy care   ☐ Comfortable   ☐ Versatile   ☐ Durable   ☐ Breathable
☐ Weather-appropriate   ☐ Easy movement   ☐ Easy to style / match
☐ Modest   ☐ Secure / doesn't require constant adjusting
☐ Affordable to replace   ☐ High quality   ☐ Low maintenance
Which qualities did you place under NON-NEGOTIABLE?
Which qualities are nice to have but not worth compromising your style for?
WHAT ARE YOU WILLING TO TRADE?

No wardrobe gives you everything in every garment. Sometimes you may choose style over convenience, comfort over appearance, versatility over uniqueness, or quality over quantity. The point is to understand your own priorities—not to audit what you own.
I'm willing to sacrifice __________________ in order to have more __________________.
I am not willing to compromise on __________________.
I'm willing to spend a little more time styling an outfit if it makes me feel much more like myself.
I'm willing to own fewer pieces if the ones I own are comfortable and versatile.
Your answer doesn't need to sound sophisticated. It just needs to be true for you.

title: Fantasy Life vs Real Life
lines: The Wardrobe You Imagined You'd Need
This is where things can get interesting.
Look at the clothes you own — or the clothes you repeatedly save, shop for, or wish you could wear.
Are some of them designed for a life you don't actually live?
- corporate clothes for a job you don't have
- party clothes for events you rarely attend
- vacation clothes for trips that happen once a year
- clothes for a version of yourself you thought you were supposed to become
This doesn't mean those clothes are bad.
It means we should notice the story behind them.
☐ Clothes for an imagined social life
☐ Clothes for an imagined version of myself
☐ Trend pieces I imagined I'd wear
The biggest “fantasy life” category in my wardrobe is:
Why do I think I bought or wanted these clothes?
How often does this situation actually occur?

My clothes need to help me:
I have accumulated / saved clothes for:
I thought I would spend more time:
«My wardrobe seems prepared for ______, but my actual life requires more ______.»
This isn't about getting rid of everything connected to your dreams.
It's about recognizing the difference between:
what your wardrobe needs to support regularly
what you might occasionally want it to support.
They just don't need equal weight.

title: What Does My Life Actually Ask of My Style?
lines: Design Around the Life You Actually Live
Look back at everything you've recorded.
«Most days, I need clothes that are ______.»
«My wardrobe needs to support ______ most often.»
«I don't need my wardrobe to be dominated by ______.»

title: Connect the Dots
lines: You're Starting to See the Whole Thing
So far, you've looked at three different things.
What you want your style to look and feel like
How your clothes need to work in your actual life
Do these three things seem to agree?
If there are contradictions, don't try to fix them yet.
That's what the next section is for.
Sometimes the most interesting part of personal style is not finding three perfectly matching answers.
It's figuring out how they can coexist.
You now have a clearer picture of the life your personal style needs to exist inside.
what you repeatedly need to dress for
where your real life differs from the life your wardrobe may have been preparing for.
Now we have all three pieces.
The next step is where we bring them together.

title: Repeated Yeses
lines: Look for qualities that appear in at least two places.
Highlight or write down 5–8 qualities that appear repeatedly.

title: Strongest Patterns
lines: A repeated preference is useful. Now go one step further: ask what that preference may tell you about how you want to dress.
You might repeatedly choose relaxed fit + simple outfits + comfortable fabrics. The deeper pattern might be: “I want my clothes to feel effortless rather than restrictive or overly constructed.”
Or feminine shapes + subtle edge + noticeable jewellery might become: “I like femininity, but I want something slightly unexpected to keep it from feeling too sweet.”
The wording is yours. These are examples of how related observations can point to a larger idea, not conclusions you have to adopt.

Don't look only for identical words. Look for similar ideas. Relaxed fit, comfortable fabrics, effortless outfits, and a casual lifestyle may point toward ease. Feminine silhouettes, sweetheart necklines, jewellery, and dresses may point toward femininity. Simple outfits, neutral colours, minimal details, and clean proportions may point toward understated simplicity.
Across my body, personality, and lifestyle discoveries, a possible connecting pattern is:
Treat these as working interpretations. You can refine them as you learn more.

title: Style Tensions
lines: Your Preferences Don't Have to Agree Perfectly
This is one of the most useful parts of the process.
Sometimes two things you want seem to contradict each other.
«“I like oversized clothes, but I don't want to look swallowed.”»
«“I like minimal outfits, but I don't want them to feel boring.”»
«“I like feminine clothing, but I don't want to look overly girly.”»
«“I want to look polished, but I don't want to look overdressed.”»
«“I like revealing pieces, but I still want the overall outfit to feel balanced.”»
They can actually tell you something important about your style.
Think about two preferences that don't always fit together easily.
But I don't want too much:
I want my clothes to feel:
NOW CHOOSE YOUR MOST IMPORTANT TENSION
This may become one of the most useful sentences in your Blueprint.

title: Style Balance
lines: You may have many qualities you like.
But your style becomes clearer when you know which qualities are central, which support them, and which are occasional.
Think of your style as having three levels.
The qualities that should appear often.
These make an outfit feel recognizably like you.
Qualities that help create the overall look.
They may not appear in every outfit, but they help shape your style.
Qualities you enjoy in smaller doses.
These can add personality without taking over everything.
If an outfit contains your core qualities, but none of your accents, can it still feel like you?

title: Translate Style Into Clothing
lines: What Do Your Words Actually Look Like?

Words such as “feminine,” “relaxed,” “polished,” or “edgy” can mean completely different things to different people. Translate your own words into clothing choices; this is about creating your own style language, not following a prescribed aesthetic.
STYLE QUALITY | WHAT IT MEANS TO ME | HOW IT MAY SHOW UP IN CLOTHING
Think about silhouettes, fit, proportions, lengths, necklines, fabrics / textures, shoes, accessories, and details.
Possible meaning: not overly constructed or restrictive.
Possible clothing expressions: relaxed trousers, softer fabrics, uncomplicated combinations, or comfortable shoes.
Possible meaning: softness or traditional feminine details, without everything needing to feel sweet.
Possible clothing expressions: a neckline, dress shape, jewellery, colour, or proportion that creates the feeling you want.

Your meaning may be different. Your version of “feminine” might be a sweetheart neckline and a mini skirt; someone else's might be a long, flowing dress. Your version of “polished” might be clean proportions and simple jewellery; someone else's might be structured tailoring.
There is no universally correct translation. The meaning comes from you.

title: Style Language Dictionary
lines: This page turns vague style words into language that is actually useful to you.
You are not trying to adopt someone else's definition of style.
You're creating a vocabulary that helps you make decisions for yourself.

title: Looking Like Me
lines: When Does an Outfit Actually Feel Like You?
An outfit can look objectively beautiful.
And still not feel like you.
Because personal style sits at the intersection of several things.
LOOK AT AN OUTFIT YOU LOVE
Choose one outfit from your inspiration set or your own wardrobe.
Does it work with the physical qualities I discovered?
Does it reflect the visual qualities I actually want?
Would this make sense for my actual life?
An outfit feels like me when it has:

title: Good on Me Is Not the Same as My Style
lines: This distinction can save you from buying a lot of clothes you don't actually want.
«Something can look good on me and still not be my style when…»
«I can admire an outfit without wanting to wear it because…»
«A flattering outfit isn't automatically a good outfit for me because…»
An outfit that looked good on me but didn't feel like me:
An outfit that may not fit a traditional style rule but felt very much like me:
You are not trying to prove that every outfit you wear is universally flattering.
You're learning what makes an outfit right for you.

title: My Style Direction
lines: From Preferences to a Point of View
You've gathered enough information now to describe the direction your style is naturally moving toward.
Don't worry about finding the perfect aesthetic label.
Instead, describe the combination of qualities.
I want my clothes to feel:
I don't want my style to feel:
My clothes need to work for:
«I want to dress in a way that feels [CORE QUALITIES], combining [QUALITY] with [QUALITY], while keeping my clothes practical for [LIFESTYLE].»

title: Make It More Specific
lines: Your Style Direction in Plain Language
Now make it sound like you, not a fashion textbook.
«I want to feel… when I get dressed.»

title: My Personal Outfit Directions
lines: You don't need a literal uniform. It can be useful to understand the types of outfit combinations that repeatedly make sense for you. These are your Personal Outfit Directions: flexible structures you can return to when you don't know what to wear.
SHAPE — What creates the overall silhouette?
BALANCE — What keeps the outfit visually balanced?
FINISH — What makes it feel complete?
BASE: simple fitted top + relaxed trousers
SHAPE: defined upper body + volume below
FINISH: earrings + watch + elevated everyday shoes
This example describes the structure of an outfit; it is not a combination you need to copy. Your own directions should come from your discoveries.

title: What I Don't Need to Become
lines: My Style Doesn't Have to Look Like Everyone Else's
There will always be clothes you're told you should own.
Aesthetic labels you're told you should fit into.
But discovering your personal style also means becoming comfortable with what isn't yours.
«I don't need to dress like __________________ to be stylish.»
«I don't need to own __________________ just because it's considered a wardrobe essential.»
«I don't need my style to look __________________.»
«I don't need to follow the fashion rule that says __________________.»
«I don't need to force myself to like __________________.»
«I give myself permission to dress in a way that __________________.»
This page matters because personal style isn't only about discovering what you like.
Sometimes it's about finally giving yourself permission to stop trying to become someone else's version of stylish.

title: Personal Style Compass
lines: Your Blueprint can help you decide whether something deserves a place in your wardrobe. Before buying something you like, pause and check it against your actual style.
0 — NO MATCH: This actively conflicts with what I know about myself.
1 — VERY WEAK MATCH: Very little about this works for me.
2 — WEAK MATCH: There are some positives, but significant concerns.
3 — UNCERTAIN: It could work, but I need to think about it.
4 — STRONG MATCH: This fits me well.
5 — VERY STRONG MATCH: This strongly reflects what I know I want and need.
01 — LIFESTYLE MATCH: Does this make sense for the life I actually live? Score: ___ / 5
02 — STYLE PERSONALITY MATCH: Does this reflect the visual qualities I actually want? Score: ___ / 5
03 — COLOUR MATCH: Does this colour integrate well with my colour direction, or am I choosing it intentionally as an exception? Score: ___ / 5
04 — PHYSICAL MATCH: Does the fit, shape, proportion, neckline, length, or comfort work for me? Score: ___ / 5
05 — STYLING POTENTIAL: Can I imagine styling this in ways that feel like me? Score: ___ / 5
21–25 — STRONG YES: This looks highly compatible with your current style and wardrobe direction.
17–20 — LIKELY YES: There is a strong case for it, but take a closer look at the lower-scoring areas.
13–16 — PAUSE & THINK: You may like the item, but something deserves more consideration.
5–12 — PROBABLY NOT WORTH BUYING: There are several areas of mismatch.
0–4 — DEFINITELY NOT FOR THIS WARDROBE: It may be beautiful, but it does not appear to serve your current style.

The score is not a law. You are allowed to buy something because you love it. The Compass is here to help distinguish “I genuinely want this” from “I like this, but it doesn't actually make sense for me.”
☐ Buy anyway — I love it enough.   ☐ Save for later.   ☐ Pass.

title: One-Glance Blueprint and How to Use Your Blueprint
lines: This is the page to save, screenshot, print, or keep on your phone. Return to it when you're getting dressed, saving inspiration, shopping, or wondering why something you love doesn't quite feel like you.
I don't need more clothes to become more stylish. I need to understand what makes clothes feel like me.

Your Blueprint is a reference point, not a test result or permanent identity. Return to it when you feel stuck getting dressed, save new inspiration, consider buying something, notice a new preference, or your lifestyle changes.
Does this work for the life I actually live?
Does this reflect what I have learned about myself?
Am I choosing this intentionally, or simply because I think I should?

Your style is allowed to evolve. You can revisit your colours, develop new signatures, and outgrow old preferences. The goal was never to find a perfect answer. It was to become better at answering: “Does this feel like me?”
